subject: Internal Medicine
stem: A 72-year-old male presents with exertional syncope and dyspnea. Physical examination reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, with delayed carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus). Echocardiography confirms severe calcific aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.7 cm². Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.explanation: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis has a dismal prognosis without intervention and requires prompt valve replacement.
Overzealous diuresis reduces preload in fixed outflow obstruction and can precipitate severe hypotension and cardiogenic shock.
Beta-blockers can depress myocardial contractility and are contraindicated in critical symptomatic aortic stenosis.

options.text: Watchful waiting with follow-up echocardiogram in 6 months
options.explanation: Once symptoms appear, median survival without replacement is <2 years.

explanation: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis classically manifests with the triad of dyspnea, syncope, and angina. Once symptoms appear, definitive valve replacement is indicated to restore survival expectancy.
objective: Recognize the clinical indications for prompt valve replacement in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
keyPoints: Severe aortic stenosis is defined by aortic valve area <= 1.0 cm².
The onset of symptoms indicates dramatic mortality risk without aortic valve replacement.

references.label: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease
